title: Oh Yes, How Soil Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain what soil is: weathered rock mixed with decomposing organic matter and living organisms. They cover how weathering (water, freeze-thaw, wind) and microbes, plants and carbonic acid form soil; soil horizons (O, A, E, B, C-type layers, bedrock, hardpan); parent material and residual, transported and cumulose soils; the soil texture triangle of sand, silt and clay and how particle size affects pores, drainage and capillary action; soil organisms from earthworms and gophers to microbes and mycorrhizal fungi; the nitrogen cycle and nitrogen fixing legumes; humus as a long-term carbon sink; and how tilling, agriculture and permafrost thaw affect carbon and climate change. The episode ends with a listener mail about the difference between a disease and a disorder.

segments.title: Book preorder promo and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck promote their upcoming book Stuff You Should Know: An Incomplete Compendium of Mostly Interesting Things, then introduce the dirty dirt episode and say soil is worn-down rock.

segments.title: How soil forms from weathered rock and organic matter
segments.summary: Soil is weathered rock broken down by wind, water and freeze-thaw, mixed with decomposing organic matter and living organisms. Carbonic acid from decaying plants helps break rock down further, and plants grow and hold soil together with roots.

segments.title: Lawns, microbes and soil pore balance
segments.summary: The hosts discuss lawn care, feeding microbes instead of aeration, and Josh's shrinking lawn. They describe ideal soil as roughly half solids and half pore space, with about half of the pores holding water.

segments.title: Soil horizons and the O, A, E and B layers
segments.summary: Soil horizons are horizontal layers. The O horizon is leaf litter, the A horizon is dark topsoil rich in organic matter, minerals and roots, the E horizon is leached light-colored soil, and the B horizon is subsoil with more silt and clay.

segments.title: Compacted clay, auger troubles and bedrock
segments.summary: Compacted clay defeated a rented two-person auger for fence posts. The hosts recommend a sledgehammer-style tool called a San Angelo tool to break up clay or rock. They describe bedrock as the Earth's outer skin, rock outcroppings, the saprolite-like weathered rock layer and hardpan.

segments.title: Parent material and soil formation types
segments.summary: Parent material is the original rock or mineral that weathers into soil. Soils can be residual, transported by glaciers, or cumulose like peat. Igneous and sedimentary parents produce different soils.

segments.title: Soil texture triangle: sand, silt and clay
segments.summary: Sand is the coarsest, silt is intermediate, and clay the finest particles. Pore sizes differ among them, affecting drainage and water retention. Silt has the best capillary action in a demonstration. Farmers can judge soil by feel and lab tests give ratios.

segments.title: Soil organisms: earthworms, gophers and mites
segments.summary: Larger animals such as moles, prairie dogs, lizards, earthworms and gophers mix and redistribute soil. Gophers are said to move about 1800 cubic meters per square kilometer per year. A square foot of forest soil can hold about 200 species of mites. A teaspoon of soil holds more microbes than there are people on Earth.

segments.title: Mycorrhizal fungi and Pando's Janet D
segments.summary: Mycorrhizal fungi form networks connecting plant roots, exchanging nutrients and water. Fungi come as saprotrophs, mutualists and parasites. The hosts discuss Janet D, a humongous fungus in Mendocino National Forest covering about 2000 acres, and contrast it with Pando, the aspen clone.

segments.title: Nitrogen cycle, nitrogen fixing and agriculture
segments.summary: Plants need nitrogen for chlorophyll and proteins. Legumes such as alfalfa and peanuts host rhizobium bacteria in root nodules that fix atmospheric nitrogen. Agriculture disrupts the cycle, and factory fertilizer replaces it. The Biggest Little Farm is recommended as a documentary.

segments.title: Humus, tilling and climate change
segments.summary: Humus locks carbon for long periods, but tilling disturbs it and releases carbon. Soils have lost about 120 petagrams of carbon since agriculture began versus over 400 petagrams from fossil fuels since 1751. Permafrost thaw and the Paris Climate Agreement carbon sink accounting are discussed. Burning plant waste is discouraged.

segments.title: Closing
segments.summary: The hosts close by urging listeners to get their hands dirty and thank humus, then sign off.
